title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
claim: Information about a target splits into unique, redundant and synergistic parts, which resolves conflations in common dichotomies of system organization.
layout: 2 panels, left Venn diagram and right triangle with labeled axes
description: Two panels. Panel (a) is a nested Venn diagram: a large pale-blue ellipse labeled I(X1,X2;Y) contains S(X1,X2;Y) at the top. Inside it, two overlapping blue ellipses show unique information U(X1;Y) and U(X2;Y) on the sides and redundancy R(X1,X2;Y) in the darker overlap. I(X1;Y) and I(X2;Y) are labeled below. Panel (b) is a large triangle with a gradient-filled corner at each vertex: magenta for Redundancy (top left), green for Synergy (top right) and blue for Unique information (bottom). Teal double-headed arrows run along and across the triangle. Gray labels on each edge name the dichotomies: Aligned/Incidental, Integration/Disintegration, Differentiation (Independent/Complementary) and Locally available/Localized. The eye goes first to the colored triangle.
caption: a) Information decomposition with two source variables $X_1$ and $X_2$, and target variable $Y$. b) The PID conceptual triangle resolves ambiguities in system dynamics. Traditional dichotomies in complex systems literature often conflate mathematically distinct properties. Integration conflates redundancy (integration-as-oneness) with synergy (complementary cooperation). Differentiation conflates unique information (strict independence) with synergy (interactive differentiation). Furthermore, locality conflates unique (singularly local) with redundant (multiply local) information, whereas synergistic representations are strictly de-localized (adapted from [ref]).
abstract: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.
